questions.q: In the lab's traced iteration flow, what does the orchestration layer do immediately after a job fails with 'device offline mid-queue' (failure mode 2)?
options: Check the failure-mode decision table (retryable, but not on the same device), apply exponential backoff, and resubmit to the next-best available device
Permanently fail the entire 150-iteration run
Immediately fall back to a classical simulator with no retry attempt
Resubmit to the exact same device immediately with no delay
questions.explain: Per Lesson 12's decision table, a device-offline failure is retryable but should route to a different device, and per Lesson 13 that retry uses exponential backoff rather than an immediate resubmission to the same (still offline) device.

questions.q: In the lab's cost model, one normal iteration (17 circuits, 1,000 shots each, Rigetti Ankaa-3 pricing) costs $20.40. If 10 of 150 iterations each incur exactly one wasted failed attempt before succeeding, what is the total run cost?
options: $20.40, since only one iteration's cost matters
$5,100.00, double-counting every iteration
$3,264.00 (150 x $20.40 for successful attempts, plus 10 x $20.40 = $204.00 in wasted retries)
$3,060.00, since failed attempts are never billed
questions.explain: 150 successful iterations cost 150x$20.40=$3,060, plus 10 wasted failed attempts at $20.40 each = $204, for a total of $3,264.00.

questions.q: In the $3,264.00 total run cost example, what percentage of total spend came specifically from wasted retry attempts, and why does the lesson say this number matters?
options: About 6.25% ($204/$3,264) -- logging it as its own line item reveals how much spend came from device failures rather than the optimization itself, which a single aggregate total would hide
100%, since the entire run cost is attributable to retries
50%, and it doesn't matter since all spend is equally 'real' cost
0%, since wasted retries are not actually billed in this scenario
questions.explain: $204/$3,264 ~= 6.25%. Without breaking this out as its own logged line item, a post-run review would only see a single total cost figure with no visibility into how much of it was avoidable waste from device failures.

questions.q: How does the lab suggest checking, in hindsight, whether a classical-simulator fallback (used when retries were exhausted) was a reasonable decision?
options: Compare the flagged simulator-estimated value against a later real-hardware re-evaluation at the same parameters; close agreement within a few standard errors suggests the fallback didn't meaningfully harm the optimization
There is no way to check this after the fact; fallback decisions can never be evaluated
Only check whether the fallback was cheaper, ignoring whether it was accurate
Assume the fallback was correct as long as the loop eventually converged, regardless of the specific values
questions.explain: Comparing the simulator fallback's value against a later real-hardware measurement at the same parameters, using the standard-error framework from Lesson 8, provides a concrete, evidence-based way to judge whether the fallback introduced a meaningful discrepancy.

questions.q: What specific fields does the lab say the operational log needs to capture for every iteration?
options: Only the cumulative total cost at the very end of the run, with no per-iteration breakdown
Only the final optimizer parameter values at the end of the run
Only whether the run as a whole succeeded or failed
Iteration number, device used, which path (success/failure) was taken, retry attempt count, cost per attempt (including failed ones), total latency, and fallback details if used
questions.explain: The lesson specifies a detailed per-iteration log (device, path taken, retry attempts, per-attempt cost including failures, latency, and fallback reasoning) as exactly the data needed to turn unexpected cost into an answerable question rather than a mystery.
